subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Third Wave: Coffee as Craft
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Third Wave: Coffee as Craft.

hook.text: In the early 2000s, a new movement treated coffee like wine—origin, variety, and process all mattered.

buildup.text: Roasters like Intelligentsia, Stumptown, and Counter Culture sourced beans directly from specific farms.

discovery.text: Third-wave shops introduced pour-over bars, single-origin menus, and flavor notes like 'blueberry' or 'jasmine.'

twist.text: Critics said it was pretentious. But it forced the industry to pay farmers more for exceptional beans.

climax.text: The third wave made coffee quality visible. Consumers learned that great coffee starts at the farm.

punchline.text: Coffee went from commodity to craft. Farmers noticed.

details.summary: The third wave, emerging in the early 2000s, treats coffee as an artisanal craft comparable to wine. It emphasizes single-origin beans, transparent sourcing, light roasting, and precise brewing. Roasters like Intelligentsia, Counter Culture, and Stumptown led the movement that now spans the globe.
details.whyItMatters: The third wave proved that coffee can be a product of terroir, skill, and intention. It connected consumers directly to farms and elevated the entire supply chain.
takeaways: The third wave treats coffee as artisanal craft
It values single-origin, transparency, and light roasting
The movement emerged in the early 2000s and is now global

faq.question: Who coined the term third wave coffee?
faq.answer: Trish Rothgeb, then a roaster at Wrecking Ball Coffee, coined the term in a 2002 article for the Roasters Guild newsletter. She defined the first wave as commodity coffee, the second wave as the Starbucks revolution, and the third wave as coffee appreciated as a craft product.

faq.question: How has the third wave changed the supply chain?
faq.answer: It created demand for traceability from farm to cup. Roasters visit farms, pay premium prices, and build long-term relationships with growers. Farmers now receive feedback on quality and have incentives to improve. The power dynamic is slowly shifting toward producers.
